title: Designing for a sales team that did not exist yet
metaTitle: A site that arms a sales conversation
excerpt: Design the sales page before the sales team exists. It should say what the product is, who it is for, what you can prove, and the next step to send.
alt: Clothes on wooden hangers suspended from a white branch against a plain wall, a small set ready to hand to someone else.
caption: A small set, hung where someone else can take it. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a sales page let someone do without a call?
faqs.answer: It should let them repeat what the product is, who it is for, and what the next step is. The proof on the page should be true and permitted. If the founder has to add a correcting paragraph every time they send the link, the page is not ready.

faqs.question: How much proof is enough before you have many customers?
faqs.answer: One true pilot, a real screenshot, or a plain account of the process is enough. A logo you are not allowed to use, or a quote you wrote yourself, will fail the first time a buyer asks. Leave a number off the page if you cannot define it.

faqs.question: When should you add more pages for a future sales hire?
faqs.answer: Add them when they are true. The hire needs the offer, how it works, and the next step. A security center and a partner program can wait until those things exist. The page is part of their onboarding, so it has to match the pitch.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
A website for a sales team has to arm a conversation. It states what the product is, who it is for, the proof you actually have, and a next step a salesperson can send. You can design that page before the team exists. You should. The first seller, even if the seller is the founder, will need a link that does not depend on their charm to finish the explanation.

If the page only makes sense after a call, the call becomes the product. Some early companies can live that way for a month. The moment a second person has to sell, the page has to hold the explanation without them in the room.

## A link they can send

Assume the message is short. "Following up, this is the page." The recipient was not in the room. They may be the buyer, or the person the buyer forwarded to. The page has to stand alone in that forward.

[Google's title-link guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/title-link) matters here because the title is often the only line in the preview. The title should say the product and who it is for, not the company slogan. When the link is pasted into a mail or a chat, the preview does the first pitch. Write the title and the share description as that pitch. Then make the first screen agree with them. A preview that promises one thing and a hero that says another makes the sender look careless.

Give the seller a single URL for the main offer. A folder of links, with a different deck for every vertical, is a later luxury. At the start, one page that is true is better than five pages that are half maintained. If a seller is editing a personal version in a doc, the site has already failed them.

The page should be readable without a login. Gating the explanation to book a meeting means the forward dies at the gate. Gate the product if you must. Do not gate the sentence.

## What it is

The first screen is a sentence a seller can say aloud and a stranger can repeat after one read. What it does, for whom, in the words the buyer uses. Then one picture of the real product, or one concrete description of the outcome if a picture would mislead.

Avoid a headline that needs the salesperson to translate it. If they always add "what we mean is," put what they mean on the page and delete the original. The translation is the copy. The clever line was the obstacle.

Keep a short paragraph under the sentence for the second reader, the one who was forwarded to. They need slightly more: the object the product works on, the moment in the day it is used, and what it replaces. Three or four lines. Not a history of the category.

Name the category only if the buyer searches that way. If they search for the job, use the job. A seller knows which phrase gets a reply. Sit with the last ten emails that got a reply and steal that phrase for the page. That is the voice. A workshop voice will not survive contact with a real thread.

## Who it is for

A sales page that is for everyone makes the seller invent the qualification on every call. Put the qualification on the page. Company size, if it matters. The role. The situation: "You already have a queue of requests and no place they live." The reader should be able to say "this is us" or "this is not us" without help.

That clarity will cost you mismatched leads. Pay the cost. A mismatched lead consumes a meeting and teaches the future sales hire the wrong pitch. The page is training material as much as it is marketing. The first hire will learn the pitch from it, and from the founder. If those two disagree, they will learn the founder's aside and ignore the site. Fix the site until the founder can send it without a paragraph of correction.

A short "not for" line helps the seller say no. "We are not a fit for teams that need on-prem this year." That line prevents a week of polite email. It also prevents the site from acquiring a feature section full of things you do not do, added because one prospect asked.

If you have two real buyers with different jobs, give them two paths on the page, with two sentences. Do not average them into a fog. A salesperson can point to the path that matches the person on the call. An averaged headline matches neither, and the seller will stop sending the link.

## Proof you can stand behind

Proof is what a skeptical forwarded reader looks for after the sentence. Use only what is true and permitted.

- A named customer, with a specific outcome you are allowed to describe, or a logo only when they have agreed.
- A screenshot of the product doing the job, with data that is not a customer's secret.
- A concrete description of how the work goes: the first call, the setup, the first week. Sequences are proof that a process exists.
- The founder's relevant experience, stated plainly, if there are no customers yet. Do not invent a customer to fill the gap.

Leave numbers off unless they are yours and defined. "Trusted by teams" with no teams is a costume. A single true pilot, described, is stronger. Down the Cove, Thomas Bewick, and the other public Hanabi projects are examples of named work a studio can point to. Your company needs its own true list, even if the list is short. A short list is a stage. A fake list is a problem the first sales hire will have to apologize for.

Quotes need a person and a permission. Do not write the quote you wish a customer had said. A seller who is asked about that quote will have to squirm, and the squirm will undo the page. If you have no quote, use the screenshot and the sequence.

## The next step

The next step should be something the seller can promise. A 30-minute call, a pilot with a defined shape, a reply to a mail. Put it on the page in the same words they use. If the button says "request a demo" and the seller says "I'll send a calendar," pick one and make the page and the habit match.

For an early company the step is often a call with the founder. Say that, if it is true. "You will talk with the founder" is a real promise and a filter. Pretending there is a team of account executives is a small lie that collapses on the first meeting. Design the page for the team you have. When the team exists, the page can say "you will talk with sales" without a rewrite of the offer.

Make the step easy to repeat. A link the seller can paste. A calendar that shows the right hours. A form that asks for the one fact the seller needs before the call, not a qualification maze. The seller should be able to say "use the link, pick a time" and then be done. If they have to attach a PDF for the page to make sense, the PDF has become the site. Fold the necessary PDF sentence into the page and keep the attachment for the security questionnaire, later.

After the call, the same URL should still be the reference. The buyer will share it internally. If your follow-up deck says a different offer, you are asking the internal champion to reconcile two stories. They will not. They will go quiet.

## Before the team exists

Design the page as the onboarding for the hire you have not made. A new seller should be able to read it on the first morning and know what they sell, who they sell it to, what they may claim, and what the next step is. If the page cannot do that, the onboarding will be a series of shadow calls and a private doc. Write the doc, then put its true sentences on the site. Do not keep the truth in a doc and the costume on the site.

Include a small set of pages the hire will eventually need, only when they are true: the main offer, a simple explanation of how it works, and a way to start. Skip the resource library, the partner program, and the enterprise security center until you have those things. A security center with nothing in it is a promise to a buyer you cannot yet serve. The next problem, when that buyer arrives, is how to answer their questions without turning the homepage into a compliance binder. That piece is [the first enterprise buyer](/blog/the-first-enterprise-buyer).

Until then, keep the page current in the same week the pitch changes. A sales team that does not exist yet cannot maintain it. The founder has to. The habit is the asset you will hand the hire.

If you want that page built so a seller can send it without a translator, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min).
